kinds.d: Loose undrilled pearl, natural or cultured, differing by the water it grew in, with size, shape and colour as options.

x.d: Pearl from wild oysters fished in the Persian Gulf off Bahrain, praised by Pliny; extremely rare and found only by opening many shells.
x.dt: no nucleus · lab report needed to prove natural origin

x.d: Saltwater cultured pearl from Pinctada fucata in Japan and China, typically 2–10 mm; large-scale cultivation began in the early twentieth century.

v.d: Granted to Tokichi Nishikawa; Mikimoto used the technology

x.dt: 2–10 mm · lustre most important · white to cream

x.d: The largest and rarest cultured pearls, from the Pinctada maxima oyster, farmed off north-western Australia.
Black cultured pearl from Pinctada margaritifera in Tahiti and other Pacific islands, one pearl nucleated at a time.
x.dt: dark body colours · one nucleus per oyster

x.d: Pearl grown in freshwater mussels; cultivation began in Lake Biwa in 1914 and China is now the commercial producer.
x.dt: tissue-nucleated · many shapes · sorted by A grades for shape, lustre, surface, colour, matching

x.d: Pearl composed entirely of nacre, formed when mantle tissue slips off the bead during culturing; small and irregular.
Cultured or natural pearl of highly irregular shape, valued for individuality.
Rare non-nacreous natural pearls from the queen conch (often pink with a flame pattern) and from the Melo bailer shell.
x.dt: no nacre · flame pattern · lacks the lustre of nacreous pearls

kinds.d: Red and pink coral skeleton of the genus Corallium, worked as beads and cabochons.

x.d: Corallium rubrum, the first described species, from the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, including the caves of Alghero in Sardinia.
x.dt: pale pink to deep red · cabochons and beads · Mohs 3.5

x.d: Other Corallium species from the western Pacific around Japan and Taiwan, at depths of 350 to 1,500 m.
Coral worked in Torre del Greco near Naples, which set up a coral society in 1790 and its first factory in 1805.

kinds.d: Black lignite gem material cut and polished for jewellery, best known as Whitby jet.

x.d: Jet from the Jet Rock near Whitby, England, about 181 million years old, made fashionable for Victorian mourning jewellery.

v.d: Fashion began after she wore it in mourning; Whitby production peaked in the early 1870s

x.dt: warm to touch · brown streak on porcelain

x.d: Jet from northern Spain, about 155 million years old, worked at Santiago de Compostela into pilgrims' amulets.
Jet used by Navajo and Pueblo peoples in New Mexico.
French jet or Vauxhall glass, ebonite (vulcanite), anthracite and bog oak, sold as jet at its peak.

brands.d: Pearl jeweller founded by Kokichi Mikimoto, who used pearl-culture technology patented by Nishikawa in 1916.
Major producer of South Sea pearls off north-western Australia.

notes: Old 'Loose pearl' became Pearl; old models Akoya, South Sea and Tahitian pearl became archetypes. CITES note left out (no retrieved page). Edison pearls omitted (page does not cover them, no source). Amber stays in Fossils. Gem labs are in shelf 01_00.
